routes.label: Examine the triangles formed by the extended sides

question:
An “\(n\)-pointed star” is formed as follows: the sides of a convex polygon are numbered consecutively \(1,\) \(2,\) \(\ldots,\) \(k,\) \(\ldots,\) \(n,\) \(n\geq5;\) for all \(n\) values of \(k,\) sides \(k\) and \(k+2\) are non-parallel, sides \(n+1\) and \(n+2\) being respectively identical with sides \(1\) and \(2;\) prolong the \(n\) pairs of sides numbered \(k\) and \(k+2\) until they meet. (A figure is shown for the case \(n=5.\))

[Figure 1](figures/1966_AMC_12_Q21_question_fig1.svg)

Let \(S\) be the degree-sum of the interior angles at the \(n\) points of the star; then \(S\) equals:
solution:
Each pair of extended sides, together with the intervening polygon side, forms a triangle. Its base angles tell us both the point angle and whether the point lies in the configuration shown.

[Figure 1](figures/1966_AMC_12_Q21_question_fig1.svg)

Let the consecutive polygon interior angles be \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n\), with cyclic indices. Let \(\theta_i\) be the angle at the intersection of the two side lines adjoining the side whose endpoint angles are \(\alpha_i\) and \(\alpha_{i+1}\). We take the angle between the rays leading back toward those two endpoints.

If \(\alpha_i+\alpha_{i+1}>180^\circ\), the intersection lies across the intervening side from the polygon. The triangle's base angles are \(180^\circ-\alpha_i\) and \(180^\circ-\alpha_{i+1}\), so
\[
\theta_i=\alpha_i+\alpha_{i+1}-180^\circ.
\]
If \(\alpha_i+\alpha_{i+1}<180^\circ\), the intersection lies on the polygon's side of that line. The triangle's base angles are now \(\alpha_i\) and \(\alpha_{i+1}\), giving
\[
\theta_i=180^\circ-\alpha_i-\alpha_{i+1}.
\]
Equality would make the two outer side lines parallel, which the question excludes. Thus, in general,
\[
\theta_i=\left|\alpha_i+\alpha_{i+1}-180^\circ\right|.
\]

Assume now that every intersection has the outward-tip configuration shown, so every adjacent angle sum exceeds \(180^\circ\). Summing the first formula counts each polygon angle twice. Since the polygon interior angles total \(180^\circ(n-2)\),
\[
S=2\cdot180^\circ(n-2)-180^\circ n
 =180^\circ(n-4).
\]
This gives choice E under that additional assumption.

The assumption need not hold. To construct a counterexample, take five tangents to a circle whose consecutive tangency points have central-angle gaps \(120^\circ,120^\circ,40^\circ,40^\circ,40^\circ\). These tangents bound a convex pentagon. The radii to consecutive tangency points are perpendicular to their tangents, so each polygon angle is \(180^\circ\) minus its corresponding central-angle gap. The consecutive interior angles are therefore
\[
60^\circ,\ 60^\circ,\ 140^\circ,\ 140^\circ,\ 140^\circ.
\]
Their adjacent sums are \(120^\circ,200^\circ,280^\circ,280^\circ,200^\circ\), none equal to \(180^\circ\), so all required side pairs are nonparallel. The point angles are
\[
60^\circ,\ 20^\circ,\ 100^\circ,\ 100^\circ,\ 20^\circ,
\]
whose sum is \(300^\circ\). By comparison, a regular pentagon has interior angles \(108^\circ\), producing five \(36^\circ\) point angles and sum \(180^\circ\).

Thus the stated construction does not determine a unique sum. The intended value is \(180(n-4)\) degrees, choice E, when the outward-tip condition is imposed.
